title: 25 — C# Performance
html:
25 — C# Performance

Code-level performance: what actually costs, how to see it, and which "optimisations" are cargo cult.

This file assumes the GC model from 16 §2 and the profiling method from 23 §8. It does not repeat them. Where they overlap, this file goes down a level — to the statements you write rather than the system you run.

1. The only rule that matters

Measure, change one thing, measure again. Every rule below is a hypothesis until your profiler agrees with it on your workload.

The three questions, in order:

Question Tool
Is this code even hot? Profiler on a realistic workload
Is it slow because of CPU, allocation, or waiting? Allocation profiler / thread stacks
Did my change help, and by how much? BenchmarkDotNet, or the same profiler run twice

⚠️ The most expensive performance work is the kind spent on code that runs twice a day. A senior engineer's first move is to find out where the time goes, not to start rewriting loops.

2. Benchmarking without lying to yourself

[MemoryDiagnoser]                       // report allocations, not just time
public class ParseBenchmarks
{
    private readonly string _line = "GB0009252882,1500.25,GBP";

    [Benchmark(Baseline = true)]
    public decimal Split() => decimal.Parse(_line.Split(',')[1]);

    [Benchmark]
    public decimal Span()
    {
        ReadOnlySpan<char> s = _line;
        int first = s.IndexOf(',');
        ReadOnlySpan<char> rest = s[(first + 1)..];
        return decimal.Parse(rest[..rest.IndexOf(',')]);
    }
}

Run it with dotnet run -c Release. Never benchmark a Debug build — the JIT skips most optimisation and the numbers are meaningless.

The four ways a microbenchmark lies:

Lie Why Fix
Dead-code elimination The JIT deletes work whose result you ignore Return the value; BenchmarkDotNet consumes it
Constant folding Inputs known at compile time get precomputed Take inputs from non-const fields
Cold start First call includes JIT and tier-0 code BenchmarkDotNet warms up; hand-rolled Stopwatch loops do not
Unrealistic data A 3-element list behaves nothing like a 3-million-element one Benchmark at production shape

⚠️ A Stopwatch around a for loop is the classic homemade benchmark and gets all four wrong. Use BenchmarkDotNet.

3. Allocation — where it actually comes from

The deep dive (16 §2.4) lists the toolkit: Span, ArrayPool, stackalloc, string.Create, struct enumerators. What follows is where allocations sneak in when nobody is looking.

3.1 Boxing, and the five places it hides

Boxing copies a value type onto the heap. It is invisible in source, so learn the shapes:

// 1. Assigning a struct to object / a non-generic interface
object o = 42;                                   // boxes

// 2. A struct implementing an interface, used through that interface
IComparable c = 42;                              // boxes

// 3. params object[] — every value argument boxes
Console.WriteLine("{0} {1}", id, count);         // 2 boxes + an array

// 4. Non-generic collections (rare now, but they exist in old code)
var list = new ArrayList { 1, 2, 3 };            // 3 boxes

// 5. Enum as a dictionary key without a comparer, on older runtimes
var d = new Dictionary<MyEnum, int>();           // fine on modern .NET; boxed on .NET Framework

The fix is almost always generics. string.Format/interpolation with a generic overload, IEquatable<T> on your struct, Dictionary<TKey, TValue> over Hashtable.

3.2 Closures capture more than you think

// Allocates a closure object per call, because `threshold` is captured
public IEnumerable<Order> Big(List<Order> orders, decimal threshold) =>
    orders.Where(o => o.Amount > threshold);

// Static lambda — no capture, cached delegate, zero allocation
public IEnumerable<Order> BigStatic(List<Order> orders) =>
    orders.Where(static o => o.Amount > 1000m);

Marking a lambda static (C# 9+) is a compile-time assertion that it captures nothing. If it accidentally captures, you get an error rather than a silent allocation. Use it wherever the lambda genuinely needs no state.

3.3 The logging trap

// BAD: formats eagerly even when Debug is disabled, allocates a string every call, loses structure
_logger.LogDebug($"Settled order {orderId} for {amount:C}");

// GOOD: no formatting unless the level is enabled; OrderId and Amount stay queryable
_logger.LogDebug("Settled order {OrderId} for {Amount}", orderId, amount);

// BEST on a hot path: source-generated, no boxing, no params array
[LoggerMessage(Level = LogLevel.Debug, Message = "Settled order {OrderId} for {Amount}")]
private partial void LogSettled(string orderId, decimal amount);

⚠️ The interpolated version is the single most common allocation bug in .NET services. The string is built before the call, so a disabled log level costs you the full formatting anyway.

4. Structs — the copies you did not ask for

public struct Money                    // NOT readonly
{
    public decimal Amount;
    public decimal Round() => Math.Round(Amount, 2);
}

public class Holding
{
    private readonly Money _value;     // readonly FIELD of a non-readonly STRUCT

    public decimal Rounded() => _value.Round();   // ⚠️ copies the whole struct, every call
}

Because Money is not readonly, the compiler cannot prove Round() will not mutate the field — so it makes a defensive copy first. The same happens with in parameters and ref readonly fields.

The fix is one keyword:

public readonly struct Money           // now the compiler knows nothing mutates
{
    public decimal Amount { get; init; }
    public decimal Round() => Math.Round(Amount, 2);
}
Guidance Reason
Prefer readonly record struct for value objects Structural equality, no defensive copies, no allocation
Keep structs ≤ ~16–24 bytes Every assignment and argument pass copies the whole thing
Never make a mutable struct Copies mutate the copy; the bug is genuinely hard to see
Use in only on readonly structs Otherwise in adds defensive copies rather than removing one

5. Collections

5.1 Pre-size when you know the size

var list = new List<Order>(orders.Count);        // one allocation
var dict = new Dictionary<string, Order>(orders.Count, StringComparer.Ordinal);

A List<T> that grows from empty to 1,000 items reallocates and copies ten times (1, 4, 8, 16 … 1024), throwing away every intermediate array. Passing the capacity removes all of it.

5.2 One lookup, not two

// Two hashes of the same key
if (dict.ContainsKey(key)) { var v = dict[key]; Use(v); }

// One
if (dict.TryGetValue(key, out var v)) Use(v);

// Zero extra lookups even for the update case (.NET 6+)
ref int count = ref CollectionsMarshal.GetValueRefOrAddDefault(counts, key, out _);
count++;                                          // writes straight into the bucket

The GetValueRefOrAddDefault form is the fastest way to write a frequency counter in C#. It is also easy to misuse: the ref is invalidated by any structural change to the dictionary, so do not hold it across an Add.

5.3 The enumerator allocation

List<Order> orders = GetOrders();

foreach (var o in orders) { }                     // struct enumerator — zero allocation

IEnumerable<Order> asInterface = orders;
foreach (var o in asInterface) { }                // boxes the enumerator — one allocation

Declaring a local or parameter as IEnumerable<T> when you have a List<T> costs an allocation per enumeration. On a hot path, type the variable concretely; everywhere else, take the readability.

5.4 Pick the right structure

Need Use Not
Membership test HashSet<T> — O(1) List.Contains — O(n)
Key → value Dictionary<K,V> List of tuples with a scan
Fixed, known at build array List<T>
Append and iterate only List<T> LinkedList<T> — worse cache locality, more allocation
Highest/lowest repeatedly PriorityQueue<T,P> Re-sorting a list

6. Strings

// O(n²) — each += allocates a new string and copies everything so far
string s = "";
foreach (var part in parts) s += part;

// O(n)
var sb = new StringBuilder();
foreach (var part in parts) sb.Append(part);
string s2 = sb.ToString();

// Better when the parts are already a collection
string s3 = string.Join("", parts);

// Best when the final length is known
string s4 = string.Create(totalLength, parts, (span, p) => { /* write into span */ });

Comparison is a correctness question before it is a performance one:

if (code.Equals(other, StringComparison.Ordinal))            // fast, exact — right for IDs, codes, keys
if (name.Equals(other, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))  // fast, case-insensitive — right for lookups
if (title.Equals(other, StringComparison.CurrentCulture))    // slow, locale-dependent — right for user-facing sort

⚠️ The default for == is ordinal, but the default for string.Compare and ToUpper() is culture-sensitive. Culture-aware comparison is both slower and, in Turkish locales, gives "I".ToLower() != "i" — the famous Turkish-İ bug. Use Ordinal for anything machine-readable, and always pass an explicit StringComparer to a dictionary keyed by a string.

7. Async

7.1 Async is not free

Every async method that actually suspends allocates a state machine box and a Task. When a method almost always completes synchronously — a cache hit, a buffered read — that cost is pure overhead.

// Allocates a Task even on the cache hit path
public async Task<Order> GetAsync(string id)
{
    if (_cache.TryGetValue(id, out var cached)) return cached;
    return await _db.LoadAsync(id);
}

// Allocates nothing on the hit path
public ValueTask<Order> GetAsync(string id) =>
    _cache.TryGetValue(id, out var cached)
        ? ValueTask.FromResult(cached)
        : new ValueTask<Order>(_db.LoadAsync(id));

⚠️ ValueTask has rules. Await it once, never .Result it, never store it. If you cannot guarantee that, use Task — a wrong ValueTask is far worse than an allocated Task. Use it for hot, usually-synchronous paths; Task everywhere else.

7.2 The two async crimes

// Sync over async — burns a thread and deadlocks under a SynchronizationContext
var order = _db.LoadAsync(id).Result;

// Async over sync — no benefit, adds a state machine and a thread-pool hop
public async Task<int> AddAsync(int a, int b) => await Task.Run(() => a + b);

Neither adds concurrency. The first removes a thread from the pool and blocks it; the second moves trivial work onto another thread and pays for the trip.

7.3 Parallel awaits

// Sequential — 300ms
var a = await GetA();
var b = await GetB();
var c = await GetC();

// Concurrent — ~100ms
Task<A> ta = GetA(); Task<B> tb = GetB(); Task<C> tc = GetC();
await Task.WhenAll(ta, tb, tc);

⚠️ Only when the calls are genuinely independent, and only where the downstream can take the concurrency. Firing fifty parallel requests at a database with a 20-connection pool makes things slower, not faster.

8. Exceptions are not control flow

Throwing and catching costs roughly microseconds — thousands of times a simple branch — because it walks the stack collecting frames.

// Terrible in a loop over 100k rows
try { value = int.Parse(text); } catch (FormatException) { value = 0; }

// Free
if (!int.TryParse(text, out int value)) value = 0;

This is not an argument against exceptions. It is an argument against using them for the expected case. Parse failures on user input are expected; a disk disappearing is not.

9. The micro-optimisations that do not matter

Things people still argue about that a profiler will never show you:

Claim Reality
i++ vs ++i Identical IL for an int local
for vs foreach over an array The JIT produces near-identical code and elides bounds checks in both
Caching list.Count in a local The JIT already hoists it
string.Empty vs "" Both are the same interned instance
Removing {} from a one-line if Zero runtime effect; costs readability
sealed on every class Real but tiny; worth it for design reasons, not speed

⚠️ Where the time actually goes, in the order worth checking: a database round trip, an N+1 query, a missing index, a network hop, serialisation of a payload far larger than needed, a lock held too long, and only then your loop. See 23 §8.3.

10. Checklist

Before claiming a change is faster:

  • Measured on a Release build with realistic data volume
  • Allocations reported ([MemoryDiagnoser]), not just elapsed time
  • Compared against a baseline, not against a memory of how it used to feel
  • The change is on a path the profiler says is actually hot
  • Readability cost is worth it — and there is a comment saying why the odd-looking version exists

Interview angle. The strongest answer to "how would you make this faster?" is never a trick. It is: "I'd profile it first — but the usual suspects in this shape of code are N+1 queries, allocation in a loop, and sync-over-async. Which of those it is changes what I'd do." That answers the question and shows you know the difference between a hypothesis and a measurement.
